title: Magha Puja again
hookLine: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind

lines: A MONK IN A PINE TREE.
WHAT IS THE HEART OF IT?
cards: A Chan monk lives up in the branches of a pine tree, so the story goes, and people call him the Bird's Nest master.

One day a governor named Bai Juyi, who is also a poet, stands underneath and calls up: that's a dangerous place to sit. The monk calls down: your seat is more dangerous than mine. Then the governor asks the big question.
What is the heart of the Buddha's teaching? And the monk in the tree answers with a verse you met on day one fifty. Today is Magha Puja, the full moon of that verse.

teach.h: ONE VERSE ON THE FULL MOON.
teach.b: In Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, Magha Puja remembers a gathering of monks and the short teaching the Buddha gave them.
One of its verses sits in the Dhammapada, and in Max Müller's words it reads: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened."
You've walked around a temple with that verse before. This year brought two more homes for it. First, the Abhidhamma, where this year began.
The Theravada's higher teaching sorts every moment of mind, and its first book opens its list of topics with one sorting: states that are skillful, unskillful, or neither.
The Pali for skillful is kusala, the same word behind Müller's to do good. So the middle of the verse is also the Abhidhamma's first cut. Then Chan.

teach.h: THE PRECEPT OF THE SEVEN BUDDHAS.
teach.b: In Chinese tradition the verse is called the shared precept of the seven Buddhas, which tradition says each Buddha of the past taught. The Bird's Nest master gives the governor the verse: do no evil, do good.

The governor is unimpressed. A child of three knows that, he says. And the monk answers, in the story as the Chan records keep it: a child of three may be able to say it, but an old man of eighty can't manage to do it.

teach.h: EASY TO SAY, HARD TO DO.
teach.b: The verse isn't hard to understand. It's hard to do, every day, and that's why each school keeps coming back to it as the heart of it.

how: In Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, Buddhists keep Magha Puja on a full moon with temple visits, giving, precepts and an evening candlelit walk around the temple, often chanting the verses of the Ovada Patimokkha.

o: a full moon remembering a gathering and a short verse
a full moon marking the Buddha's first sermon
the night monks begin their rains retreat

games.q: one verse, three homes: tap the pairs.
p: the full moon of the verse
the monk who lives in a pine tree

s: the governor called the verse too deep to understand
he said a child of three knows it.
in China the verse is honored as the shared precept of the seven Buddhas
taught, tradition says, by each Buddha of the past.
kusala, in the verse, is also a word the Abhidhamma uses to sort moments of mind
skillful, unskillful and neither is the first cut it makes.

games.q: you're the governor. the monk in the tree tells you the heart of the teaching: do no evil, do good. what do you say?
o: nothing; you bow and walk away.
games.why: Bai Juyi says a child of three knows it. the monk answers that an old man of eighty still can't do it.

practice: Let the breath settle like a glass of water left alone, the verse's third part.

When it's a little clearer, choose one small harm you'll skip, child-sized, something a three-year-old could understand, and one small good thing you'll do, also child-sized. Then let both rest, and come back to the clearing water.

wordCard.voice: Magha Puja. The full moon remembering the gathering of monks and the verse: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind, carried by Theravada, the Abhidhamma and Chan alike. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali kusala: skillful, wholesome; the 'do good' of Dhammapada 183 and the Abhidhamma's first sorting word.

carryVoice: Your line: the heart of it. Easy to say, hard to do. Until tomorrow.
